newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: S.Korea strikes -- ILO writes to President Kim.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea strikes -- ILO writes to President Kim.

text.p: The head of the International Labour Organisation has written to South Korean President Kim Young-sam after a global trade union group asked him to intervene to prevent Seoul arresting strike leaders, an ILO spokesman said on Friday.
Five union groups, including the International Metalworkers' Federation, said meanwhile that they had delivered a letter of protest on Friday to South Korea's diplomatic mission in Geneva.
ILO spokesman Michel Barton said that the freedom of trade unions was a fundamental principle of the United Nations agency, which promotes basic workers' rights in its 174 member states.

South Korea, which joined the ILO in 1991, has twice in recent years been reprimanded by an ILO committee for arrests of trade unionists and non-recognition of trade unions in violation of ILO principles of freedom of association.
The ILO spokesman declined to give details of the letter sent on Thursday by ILO director-general Michel Hansenne to Kim.

Hansenne, a former Belgian minister of social affairs, had received a message from the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) on Thursday expressing concern about possible imminent arrests of the leaders of nationwide strikes in South Korea.
"I can confirm the director-general has sent a personal message to President Kim," Barton told a news briefing in Geneva. "The contents of the letter are confidential."
"We hope the message will be taken for the good faith message that it is, and has an impact," he later told Reuters.
Barton told reporters that the two previous South Korean cases condemned by ILO's Committee on Freedom of Association were "very closely tied in theme to the situation at hand".

After complaints by unions, ILO's Committee on Freedom of Association called on South Korea in 1994 and 1996 to release or drop charges against trade unionists including Kwon Young-Kil, president of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.
Kwon and six deputies, who have taken refuge in a Seoul cathedral, on Friday rebuffed police trying to deliver a summons for them to appear in court.
The seven militant leaders have warned the authorities that any attempt to seize them would trigger nationwide work stoppages, including a public-sector shutdown.

The four other unions which delivered the joint protest letter to the South Korean mission were: the international unions of food and allied workers' associations, clerical workers, public services, and construction workers.
